planting.note: Sow fresh seed directly where it will grow in autumn so it winters over and chills naturally; this taprooted umbellifer resents transplanting once its root is established.

directions: One of the earliest bloomers in Garry oak savanna and Puget prairie turf, this low taprooted perennial sends up flat yellow umbels in late winter to early spring well before the surrounding grasses green up. It thrives in shallow, rocky or gravelly soils that bake dry over summer and wants nothing more than to be left alone once rooted in. Sow seed in fall into its permanent spot so it experiences a full winter of cold, damp chilling; germination the following spring is often slow and staggered. Established plants need almost no summer irrigation and resent heavy, wet garden soils.

planting.note: Plant corms 3-4 inches deep in fall into lean, fast-draining soil in full sun; corms multiply slowly into dense clumps over several seasons.

directions: This corm-forming geophyte sends up wiry stems topped with loose clusters of pale to deep blue-violet, star-shaped flowers in late spring, right as Garry oak meadows reach peak bloom alongside camas and brodiaeas. It goes fully dormant and disappears underground through the dry summer months, so mark its location before it vanishes. Plant corms in autumn in open, grassy sites that drain well, and avoid any summer watering that could rot the resting corm. Division of established clumps every few years keeps plantings vigorous.
sources: Native Plant Society of British Columbia

planting.note: Direct sow in fall into its permanent, well-drained site; deep taproots make this species very difficult to move once seedlings are a season old.

directions: A big, coarse-leaved relative of arrowleaf balsamroot distinguished by its broader, triangular (deltoid) basal leaves, this species forms bold clumps of sunflower-like yellow blooms in open Garry oak meadows and grassy balds through late spring. Like its cousin it grows from a thick, deep taproot that stores moisture through the dry Pacific Northwest summer, so established plants shrug off drought once their root system matures over the first two to three years. Give it full sun and rocky or gravelly soil, and start it from fall-sown seed directly in place rather than attempting to transplant older plants. It pairs naturally with native bunchgrasses and camas in a restored prairie planting.

planting.note: Nick or sand-scarify the hard seed coat before sowing in fall; this legume forms a deep taproot and prefers direct sowing over transplanting.

directions: A robust, short-lived perennial lupine of Willamette Valley and Puget lowland prairie remnants, producing tall spikes of blue-violet pea flowers above palmate leaves through late spring. It occupies the slightly moister edges and swales within Garry oak savanna, tolerating more soil moisture than many prairie companions while still demanding full sun and sharp drainage in winter. Scarify seed to break its hard coat and sow in fall or early spring; as a legume it fixes its own nitrogen and performs poorly on rich, fertilized ground. This species serves as a larval host plant for several native blue butterflies, making it a valuable addition to restoration and pollinator plantings.

planting.note: Broadcast seed in fall onto lean, well-drained soil in full sun; established tufts can also be divided and transplanted in early spring.

directions: This fine-leaved, blue-green bunchgrass is the dominant native grass of Puget lowland prairies and the open understory between widely spaced Garry oaks, forming dense evergreen tussocks that stay attractive year-round. It is the preferred host grass for several hemiparasitic prairie wildflowers and provides larval habitat for native prairie butterflies, making it a cornerstone species for oak savanna restoration. Sow seed in fall onto exposed, lean mineral soil, since it struggles to establish through thick thatch or in rich garden beds. Once established it needs no supplemental summer water and resents heavy clay that stays wet through winter.
sources: Native Plant Society of British Columbia

planting.note: Broadcast seed onto bare mineral soil in fall; tolerates heavier, seasonally damp ground better than most companion prairie bunchgrasses.

directions: A tussock-forming cool-season grass common across Garry oak savanna and Puget Sound wet prairies, recognizable by its twisted, hairy leaf blades and unusual hidden seed heads produced near the base of the clump as well as the visible ones above. It tolerates winter-wet, seasonally saturated soils far better than the drier-site fescues it often grows alongside, making it useful for the damper swales within an oak savanna planting. Sow seed in fall directly onto open ground, since like most native bunchgrasses it establishes poorly when competing with thick turf or heavy mulch. Mow or burn occasionally in late summer to mimic the historic fire regime that kept Garry oak prairies open.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep in fall into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; keep away from vegetable gardens or livestock pasture since every part is highly toxic.

directions: Grasslike basal leaves give rise in mid to late spring to a spike of small, creamy white, star-shaped flowers, blooming in Garry oak meadows at the same time as the much larger, edible camas it is dangerously easy to confuse with. All parts of the plant, including the bulb, are potent neurotoxins, so this is strictly an ornamental or restoration subject and must never be planted where it could be mistaken for an edible bulb or grazed by animals. Plant bulbs shallowly in fall in open, well-drained prairie or rock-garden soil and let it go summer-dormant without irrigation. It is increasingly offered by specialty native-plant nurseries for habitat restoration and pollinator meadow plantings where its early bloom supports native bees.

planting.note: Scatter seed on the soil surface in fall or very early spring; needs light and cool, moist conditions to germinate and self-sows readily once established.

directions: This small, wiry annual produces whorls of two-toned flowers along its stem, the upper lip white and the lower lip deep violet-blue, carpeting open patches and the dappled edges of Garry oak groves in early to mid spring. It germinates with fall and winter rains and completes its life cycle before the summer drought sets in, so seed should be sown shallowly in autumn and left undisturbed through winter. It does best with light shade from scattered oak canopy or taller grasses rather than the hottest, most exposed parts of a meadow. Once established in a planting it self-seeds freely, forming drifts that return each spring.
sources: Native Plant Society of British Columbia

planting.note: Direct sow in fall so seedlings establish over winter; tolerates light frost and thrives in the thin, rocky soils typical of oak savanna openings.

directions: One of the showiest spring annuals of Garry oak meadows and coastal bluffs, this species produces dense, rounded heads of small pink to rose flowers atop slender stems, often blanketing entire hillsides in a haze of color during April and May. It germinates with autumn rains, overwinters as a low rosette, and races to bloom and set seed before the ground dries out in summer, so it needs a site with sharp drainage and no competition from vigorous perennial turf. Direct sow in fall onto bare or thinly vegetated soil and avoid summer watering, which can rot it after it has naturally senesced. It reseeds readily where happy, making it a reliable return bloomer in a restored prairie or wildflower meadow.
sources: Native Plant Society of British Columbia

planting.note: Sow seed in fall in close contact with the roots of an established native bunchgrass host, such as Roemer's fescue; this hemiparasite performs poorly without a host plant nearby.

directions: Clusters of bristly, hairy bracts in vivid orange-red make this perennial a signature wildflower of Garry oak prairies around Puget Sound and Vancouver Island, blooming through late spring alongside camas and native lupines. Like other paintbrushes it is hemiparasitic, tapping into the roots of neighboring grasses and forbs for part of its water and nutrients, so seed should be sown or seedlings planted directly beside an established native bunchgrass such as Roemer's fescue rather than in isolation. Give it full sun, open soil, and consistent but moderate moisture through the spring growing season, tapering off as it goes dormant in summer. Because of its host dependency it establishes most reliably from locally sourced seed sown into existing prairie turf rather than as a container specimen in cultivated garden soil.
sources: Native Plant Society of British Columbia
